passage:
Monday. Seema stepped off the night bus in Chennai with her bag held in front of her. She asked the auto driver where the guesthouse lane was, then the flower seller, then the man at the tea stall. Two pointed left, one right. She followed the two, and checked once more at the corner shop.
Wednesday. A stranger said, "Come, I'll show you a shortcut." She thanked him, said she would ask at the shop, and did.
Friday. Her colleague Jahnavi laughed at her list of directions. "Three people? Two of them would have done." But the route was correct every time.

qa.q: How many people did Seema ask on Monday for the guesthouse lane?
qa.a: Seema asked the auto driver, the flower seller and the man at the tea stall.

qa.q: What was Seema probably feeling when the stranger offered a shortcut on Wednesday?
qa.a: She was probably cautious and a little uneasy, since she thanked him and chose to check at the shop instead.

qa.q: What did Seema do to reduce the risk of a wrong turn?
qa.a: She asked several people, compared their answers and checked again at the corner shop, keeping her bag in front.

qa.q: How might Jahnavi see Seema's habit of asking three people?
qa.a: Jahnavi finds it funny and says two would do, but sees that Seema's routes were correct each time.

grounding: Shows a traveller asking several people for directions, checking answers against each other and keeping valuables close over several days.

passage: Beta, I am Mehak, and at twenty-four I travelled to Varanasi with a fellow traveller, Dhruv, who said, "Ask one person, everyone is friendly." Many are, but I asked three people for the way to the ghat: a chaiwala, a shop owner and a woman selling flowers. Two answers matched, and one man who had joined us said he would take us by a different lane. It was longer, and crowded. My bag was zipped and in front of me. At the end of the lane, Dhruv put his hand to his back pocket and found it empty. I checked answers against each other after that, and Dhruv never again trusted a single voice.

qa.q: How many people did Mehak ask for the way to the ghat?
qa.a: Mehak asked three people for the way to the ghat, a chaiwala, a shop owner and a woman selling flowers.

qa.q: What was Mehak probably feeling when a man joined them and offered a different lane?
qa.a: Mehak was probably cautious and alert, since the bag was zipped and held in front and the answers had been checked against each other.

qa.q: What choice by Mehak made the journey safer?
qa.a: Mehak asked several people, checked their answers against each other and kept the bag zipped and in front.

qa.q: How might Dhruv's view of asking for directions have changed after the pocket?
qa.a: Dhruv learned that friendly help is common but one voice may not be enough, and he stopped trusting a single answer.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling a traveller who asked several people, compared answers and kept valuables close, against a companion who trusted one voice.
